advisor.summary: The gap between elective deferrals plus employer money and the §415(c) annual-additions ceiling — $72,000 for 2026 — can be filled with non-Roth after-tax employee contributions and then converted immediately, either through an in-plan Roth rollover under §402A(c)(4) or by rollover to a Roth IRA. After a maxed $24,500 deferral and typical employer contributions, that moves $30,000–$45,000 or more per year into Roth status. There is no current deduction — after-tax means after-tax — so the record is advisory: the value is decades of tax-free growth, not a line on this year's return. Unlike the IRA backdoor, the §408(d)(2) pro-rata rule does not reach this play: the plan accounts for the after-tax subaccount separately, and Notice 2014-54 lets basis and earnings split cleanly at rollover. The two gating questions are always the plan document and, in staff plans, ACP testing.
mechanics: Capacity equals the $72,000 §415(c) ceiling (2026) minus elective deferrals minus employer contributions — for example, a $24,500 deferral plus $12,500 of employer money leaves $35,000 of after-tax room.

The plan document must permit both non-Roth after-tax employee contributions and in-plan Roth conversion (or in-service distribution of the after-tax account); most off-the-shelf documents allow neither, so read first and amend if needed.
Convert immediately: earnings accrued between contribution and conversion are taxable at conversion, and a same-payroll automatic sweep — many providers offer one — keeps the taxable slice near zero.

In plans with staff, after-tax contributions are tested under the §401(m) ACP test; heavy owner use against low staff participation fails the test and gets refunded — an owner-only solo 401(k) has no ACP test and is the cleanest chassis.

The §408(d)(2) pro-rata fraction that haunts the IRA backdoor does not apply: the plan's separate accounting for the after-tax subaccount, combined with the Notice 2014-54 allocation rules, sends basis to Roth and earnings to pre-tax cleanly.

authority.note: The $72,000 annual-additions ceiling (2026) whose unused headroom after-tax contributions fill.
Authorizes in-plan Roth rollovers, including otherwise nondistributable amounts — the conversion leg.
The ACP nondiscrimination test that applies to employee after-tax contributions in plans with staff.
The IRA pro-rata rule — cited to document why it does not reach plan-level after-tax conversions.
Permits allocation of pre-tax and after-tax amounts among simultaneous rollover destinations — the clean basis-separation authority.
In-plan Roth rollover guidance covering nondistributable amounts and plan-amendment requirements.
The 2026 dollar limits used here: $24,500 deferral and $72,000 annual additions.

requirements: A 401(k) document permitting after-tax contributions and prompt conversion — amend or restate if absent; solo plans should sit with a provider whose document includes both.
Surplus cash flow after deferrals and employer contributions are already maxed, since these dollars produce no deduction.
An owner-only plan, or a staff plan the TPA projects will pass ACP testing with the owner's after-tax dollars included.
A provider or process that converts every payroll, ideally automatically.
risks: ACP failure is the leading testing risk in plans with employees: the owner's after-tax dollars come back as refunds, unwinding the year — have the TPA project the test before funding, not after.
Conversion lag quietly builds a tax bill: earnings that accrue in the after-tax account before conversion are taxable when finally moved.
Contributing after-tax dollars a plan does not actually permit is an operational failure requiring correction under the EPCRS framework of Rev. Proc. 2021-30.
Recurring legislative proposals target after-tax conversions; funded-and-converted dollars have historically been grandfathered, which argues for using capacity while it exists.
stateNotes: Conformity: after-tax contributions are in state income the year earned, and qualified Roth distributions are excluded in states that conform to federal AGI — so state treatment generally tracks federal automatically.
No PTET interaction — after-tax employee contributions create no entity-level deduction for a pass-through entity tax election to leverage.
Missouri conforms through RSMo §143.121; converted earnings, if any, are Missouri income in the conversion year, and qualified Roth distributions escape Missouri tax just as they do federally.
reviewChecklist: Plan or adoption-agreement language for after-tax contributions and in-plan conversion verified in writing — or the amendment executed — before any funding.
Current-year capacity computed ($72,000 minus deferrals minus employer contributions) and refreshed whenever employer amounts change.
Staff plans: TPA ACP projection in the file before the owner funds.
Automatic or calendared conversion process in place so earnings exposure stays near zero.
Conversion 1099-R reconciled — only post-contribution earnings show as taxable.

client.teaser: Move an extra $30,000 or more each year into savings the IRS never taxes again.
client.headline: Supercharge your Roth: tens of thousands more each year, tax-free for good
plainEnglish: A Roth account is the best deal in retirement saving. The money grows for decades, and you never pay tax on it again. The problem is the front door is small. Normal Roth deposits cap out at a few thousand dollars, and high earners are shut out.

Inside a 401(k) there is a much bigger door. The law allows total plan deposits of up to $72,000 a year, if your plan accepts a special extra type of deposit. We move those dollars to the Roth side right away, where they grow tax-free for good.

These extra deposits do not cut this year's tax bill. You fund them with money you already paid tax on. The payoff comes later, and it compounds: decades of growth the IRS never touches, and no forced withdrawals on the government's schedule.
client.analogy: It is like learning the building has a freight elevator. Same destination as the small one everyone crowds into — but it moves far more per trip.
benefits: Move an extra $30,000 to $45,000 a year into never-taxed-again savings
Works even when your income is too high for a regular Roth
No forced withdrawals later — the money compounds on your schedule
steps: WE check your plan for the two features this needs, and fix the document if it lacks them.
WE compute your exact extra room for the year.
YOU fund the extra deposits from cash flow after your normal 401(k) money is maxed.
WE set conversions to run automatically, so growth is tax-free from day one.
clientCommitments: Fund these deposits with after-tax cash — they do not lower this year's bill
Keep the automatic conversion running; never let deposits sit unconverted
Tell us when employer contributions change so we can re-size your room
